source.title: Beyond the Hard Budget: Sparsity Regularizers for More Interpretable Top-k Sparse Autoencoders
source.citation: Nathanaël M. A. Jacquier et al., 2026
source.authors: Nathanaël M. A. Jacquier; Maria Vakalopoulou; M. Hosseini

page_placements.theme: SAE width, sparsity, architecture, regularizers and supervision change latent monosemanticity

record.tranche_reason: The study compares regularized and unregularized Top-k sparse autoencoders using monosemanticity and related interpretability measures, a different method from directly identifying mixed-selectivity neurons in the original network.
record.gate_note: The study measures SAE latent monosemanticity, class purity, and reconstruction; it does not measure polysemanticity in the underlying frozen encoders’ own neurons. Reported regularizer-strength values used for selection are not recorded as findings. Numerical class-purity rows below include binary purity only; weighted-purity results are summarized in rows_left_out.
record.test_reason: The study relies on polysemanticity and superposition only as motivation and reports how its own regularizers improve Top-k SAE latents. Its monosemanticity and purity scores describe SAE dictionary latents trained on frozen encoder embeddings. It never measures polysemanticity in the encoders' own neurons (CLIP, SigLIP2, ViT-L/16) or in any classifier or language-model MLP. The rows are comparisons of the study's own method against an unregularized baseline tool, not measurements of the phenomenon in model neurons.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that both pre-selection regularizers improve Top-k SAE interpretability (monosemanticity, class purity) without reconstruction loss, and that Reg. 1 gives the larger gains. Reg. 2 concentrates the code, improving robustness to inference-time k and small-budget probing. Their central claim is that hard and soft sparsity are complementary. Two caveats: reconstruction parity is enforced by the λ selection rule, and SigLIP2 ImageNet Reg. 2 shows marginal monosemanticity decreases.
record.recipe_differences: Introduces two pre-Top-k activation regularizers for vision SAEs; it does not reproduce the original neuron-identification or feature-visualization method.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured monosemanticity and purity vary with encoder, dataset, k, and regularizer. SigLIP2 ImageNet with Reg. 2 is an exception to the general mean-monosemanticity increase; SigLIP2 at k=128 with Reg. 2 has a minor binary-purity regression noted by the authors.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding a pre-selection off-support ℓ1 or ℓ1/ℓ2 penalty to Top-k SAEs on frozen vision embeddings raises the latents' mean MonoScore and class purity at matched R². Reg. 1 gains more (e.g. ViT ImageNet k=32: 0.346→0.474). SigLIP2 ImageNet Reg. 2 is flat or marginally lower.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparsity regularization of SAE dictionaries increases monosemanticity of SAE latents (tool-level, not network neurons).

fits_no_version.finding: Baseline SAE latents lose semantic coherence away from their top activations; Reg. 1 latents stay coherent down to the bottom-10 activations (qualitative, ViT-L/16 k=32).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latent coherence differs across the activation range, and regularization extends coherence to weak activations.

record.problems: The main reported quantitative results are means over three seeds; standard deviations are in appendix tables. The authors select regularizer strength using validation reconstruction and monosemanticity. Qualitative full-range inspection is limited to selected ViT-L/16 examples. Results concern SAE latents, not individual neurons in the underlying frozen vision encoders.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 median monosemanticity, reconstruction values per individual encoder/dataset/k, dead-neuron counts, and class-purity weighted-purity values are not individually extracted. Table 2 binary-purity rows are included; weighted purity is omitted because the 60-row limit is reached if these additional configuration-level results are added. Other omitted results include cross-dataset transfer (Figure 3, Table A5), inference-time-k robustness (Figure 7, Appendix Figure A1), truncated-code probing (Figure 7 and Table 3), active-unit-mask dead-neuron ablation (Table 4), and full versus off-support ℓ1 comparison (Figure 8); these concern related SAE behaviors but are not needed for the extracted version verdicts.

untested.parts: No measurement of InceptionV1 or any classifier neurons responding to unrelated inputs.
Superposition is cited as the explanation (Elhage et al.) but not tested.
No test of initialization, regularization or noise as causes in models with spare capacity.
Changes in network-neuron polysemanticity with activation function, architecture or regularization are not measured; only SAE latents are.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not revisited.
Does not compare how polysemanticity verdicts for network neurons shift with the activation range examined or the explanation-scoring method.

record.verdict_notes: The reader marked V5 and V7 as tested, but every row measures SAE latents, which are the interpretability tool, not neurons of the models the claim concerns. I reclassified the study as T4, and no verdicts are given. Neither original source applies.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether neurons in image classifiers such as InceptionV1 respond to unrelated image inputs.
No language models, token responses, or language-model MLP neurons are studied.
Does not test whether superposition or a feature-to-neuron capacity imbalance causes polysemanticity.
Does not test initialization or training noise as causes, nor whether there is enough capacity for every feature.

Tests sparsity regularizers on Top-k SAE latents over frozen vision-model embeddings. Does not compare activation functions or underlying network architectures, measure the share of polysemantic neurons in the original encoders, or establish that every regularizer improves every setting.
Does not revisit the canonical mixed-selectivity neurons in the original networks to establish that they detect one shared feature.

Qualitatively compares top, middle, and bottom activating images for selected ViT-L/16 SAE units and reports the full-range pattern. Does not compare alternative explanation-scoring methods or systematically quantify polysemanticity separately at each activation range.

rows.subject: CLIP ViT-L/14 SAE
rows.stage_stated: SAE trained on frozen CLIP embeddings
rows.operation_detail: Train with Regularizer 1 (off-support ℓ1); compare with unregularized Top-k SAE.
rows.uncertainty: Means over 3 seeds; SD reported in Appendix Table A3.
rows.check: Mean MonoScore of SAE latents, regularized vs unregularized Top-k SAE. This compares the study's own method with a baseline. It is not the share of polysemantic neurons in a network, so it does not bear on V5. R14 (0.586 vs 0.586) and R16 (0.575 vs 0.576) are the authors' two marginal SigLIP2 ImageNet Reg. 2 exceptions.

relation.reason: Polysemanticity and superposition appear only as motivation in the introduction. The reader's earlier call of tests/T2 is not supported.

tranche.reason: The paper uses SAEs as a tool and reports only how its own regularizers perform. It measures monosemanticity of SAE latents trained on frozen embeddings, not polysemantic neurons in the encoders.

source_check.notes: All 9 rows match Tables 1 and 2. The text scrambles the table layout, but the cells place cleanly by column order and match the authors' prose on the SigLIP2 Reg. 2 exceptions. The rows score SAE dictionary latents (mean MonoScore, class purity), not the share of polysemantic units in the encoders, so versions none and T4 stand. Reg. 1 R2 is 0.001 below baseline in three configs (CLIP IN k=32, SigLIP2 OI k=128, ViT OI k=32).

statements.correction: Optional clarification: ViT ImageNet k=32, Reg. 1 (off-support l1): Mµ 0.346 to 0.474, R2 0.776 vs 0.780; Reg. 2 at the same setting: Mµ 0.414, R2 0.800. SigLIP2 ImageNet Reg. 2 Mµ: 0.586/0.586 (k=32), 0.576/0.575 (k=64), 0.560/0.561 (k=128).
statements.problem: Correct as stated. Minor precision point: the 0.346 to 0.474 example is Reg. 1 (off-support l1), but the statement names both penalties and does not say which one this is. 'Matched R2' means no R2 loss; Reg. 2 R2 is often higher (ViT ImageNet k=32: 0.800 vs 0.776).
